inline.s: As rich as a prince, you call it joy, I call it sorrow: / the seeker bears much suffering, the getter dreads the fall. / Ha! Plain fare beats delicacies, a patchwork robe is like brocade. / Heaven and earth are my cottage, why build a mansion tall? / Therefore cross out at one stroke house, land, and field.

As rich as a prince, you call it my joy and I call it sorrow. In seeking it I bear every kind of hardship; having gained it, I dread the fall. Ha! Coarse tea and plain fare beat delicacies, and a patchwork robe and worn coat are like brocade. Between heaven and earth is my house; why build a mansion tall? Therefore cross out at one stroke house, land, and field.

[You call it joy, I call it sorrow] You think that if I were as rich as a prince I would be exceedingly happy, and you do not know the suffering within it: in pursuing wealth I bear every kind of hardship; and once I have grown rich by some stroke of luck, I live in constant fear of officials, thieves, floods, fires, and spendthrift sons destroying my wealth. [Sheng shou] To suffer hardship; to toil.

blocks.text: 6. The Chapter on Talent and Learning

inline.s: The sea of learning flows on long, the ranks of letters flash to the Dipper and the Ox; / you roam at will through a hundred arts, and a gallon of wine to a thousand poems. / Ha! With brocade and embroidery filling your breast, why boast aloud? / Before birth and death, not half a point can save you. / Therefore cross out at one stroke writings that cover the world.

The sea of learning flows on without ever resting; the light of the literary world flashes to the Dipper and the Ox; you roam at will through a hundred arts, a gallon of wine to a thousand poems. Ha! With brocade and embroidery filling your breast, why boast aloud? Before birth and death, not even a thread of it can save you. Therefore cross out at one stroke writings that cover the world.
[The sea of learning] Yang Xiong of the Han, in the Fayan

"Learning and Practice": "The hundred streams learn from the sea and so reach the sea; the hills learn from the mountain and do not reach the mountain." This means that the hundred streams flow on without resting, and so reach the sea, while the hills stand still and do not move, and so do not reach the mountain. Learning should therefore be like a river flowing to the sea, advancing without cease day by day. [The ranks of letters] The literary world.
[The ranks of letters flash to the Dipper and the Ox] A description of how high this person's talent and learning are: in the literary world his radiance fills the sky
, reaching the Dipper mansion (the Northern Dipper) and the Ox mansion (the Cowherd star).

blocks.text: 7. The Chapter on Pleasure and Play

inline.s: Spring outings and summer delights, in song-and-dance halls joys come thick; / mist and rain bewilder the flowers and willows, chess and wine please kin and friends. / Ha! Before your eyes you flaunt your gallantry, but bitterness follows after. / What a pity the wasted hours, and shame-faced you turn your head in vain. / Therefore cross out at one stroke the mood of wind and moon.

Summer enjoyment and spring outings; in song-and-dance halls joys come thick and fast; mist and rain bewilder the flowers and willows; tea, wine, the lute, and chess please kin and friends. Ha! Before your eyes each flaunts his gallantry, but bitterness returns upon oneself after death. What a pity to waste the hours and miss the great matter of birth and death; in shame and remorse you turn your head in vain. Therefore cross out at one stroke the mood of wind and moon.

[Yan di] Before the eyes, at present, now. [Feng liu] Both achievement and literary grace. [Mo luo (mo luo)] A Sanskrit word, translated into Chinese as "shame." [Kong hui shou] To look back on bygone things: all was in vain.

Time passes swiftly and human life is impermanent. Students of the Buddha must be vigilant at every moment; never take things lightly, dallying in play, wasting the hours, and so knowing endless regret. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's "Verse to Admonish the Assembly" says:
"This day is gone, and with it life has dwindled, as a fish in dwindling water — what
(what)
joy is there? Great assembly: strive with diligence, as though your head were on fire! Only contemplate impermanence
(only contemplate the coming of death)
, and never give way to heedlessness
(never abandon yourself to indulgence)
[A fish in dwindling water] A fish in a pond whose waters daily run dry.
[Strive with diligence, as though your head were on fire]
When a great fire blazes upon your head and death presses swiftly near, you should recite the Buddha's name with
unflagging diligence,
quickly
and
with all urgency put out this fire of death, seizing the moment before unconsciousness and death to accomplish ten successive thoughts sustained until it becomes second nature (see in detail the
Conditions for Rebirth

article). [Impermanence] Having no permanence (all dharmas of the world arise and cease, shifting and flowing, not abiding for a single instant); it also means death, or the ghost that snatches away the soul. [Never give way to heedlessness] Never abandon yourself to indulgence and so waste your spirit and your hours. The Buddha said:
"Though for one lifetime you toil and suffer, in but a moment you are afterward born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where joy is without limit."
(The Buddha Speaks of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life)
Truly it is said:
In life you spend a thousand thoughts and ten thousand schemes, / in death you leave behind two empty hands.
Grief and joy, parting and meeting, clamor day after day; / long life or early death, want or wealth, busy every day.
Do not struggle for strength and contend for victory; / a hundred years are all a theater stage.
In a moment the gong and drum fall silent; / who knows where the exit lies.
[In a moment the gong and drum fall silent]
In the blink of an eye impermanence arrives, and this opera is sung out (the gong and drum fall silent).
